Q: Which is the best data type for createdDate and modifiedDate for mongo collection to store dates in database of spring boot application with java 17 A:

Use Instant or ZonedDateTime. Do not use LocalDateTime.

ZonedDateTime adds additional abilities about conversion between geographical zones. Therefore ZonedDateTime is a better choice only if you have to handle zone conversions within your backend. If not then Instant is my default choice as it is the simplest one. Instant handles the reading of the dates with times from your mongodb and their exposure in the standard ISO 8601 format in the controller endpoint without any additional effort.

LocalDateTime means date and time in the locale of your backend application which is generally not UTC. Using LocalDateTime would require to handle painful additional conversions to account for the time zone of the backend application.

Q: How do i show text based on the button user clicked A:

Your issue is that element in the forEach loop is a DOM button element, not an array index. You need to map each button to its corresponding content object.

HTML structure needed:

<button class="choices" data-section="history">History</button> <button class="choices" data-section="goals">Goals</button> <button class="choices" data-section="team">Team</button> <button class="choices" data-section="values">Values</button> <button class="choices" data-section="why">Why</button> <div class="mainInfo"> <h2></h2> <p></p> </div>

JavaScript solution:

constcontentMap = { history: { title: "Our History", paragraph: "As a company we thrive..." }, goals: { title: "Our Goals", paragraph: "Our goals are as follows..." }, team: { title: "Our Team", paragraph: "Our Team consists of..." }, values: { title: "Our Values", paragraph: "The values we protect..." }, why: { title: "Why Choose Us", paragraph: "The Why is one of our..." } }; constbuttons = document.getElementsByClassName("choices");consttitleElement = document.querySelector(".mainInfo h2");constparagraphElement = document.querySelector(".mainInfo p"); Array.from(buttons).forEach(button => { button.addEventListener('click',function() { constsectionKey =this.dataset.section; // Gets "history", "goals", etc. constcontent = contentMap[sectionKey]; titleElement.textContent = content.title; paragraphElement.textContent = content.paragraph; }); });

How it works step by step:

  1. Each button has a data-section attribute storing its identifier ("history", "goals", etc.)

  2. this.dataset.section extracts that identifier when clicked (e.g., "history")

  3. contentMap[sectionKey] looks up the matching content object

  4. .title and .paragraph properties update the DOM elements

Why this approach is better than alternatives:

  • No fragile index calculations

  • No need to modify existing class structure

  • Direct semantic mapping (button label matches data key)

  • Easy to add/remove buttons (just add data-section)

  • No CSS class toggling required

The dataset API automatically converts data-section to dataset.section, providing clean access to custom data attributes.

Q: MySQL client/server: TCP response packet with ACK flag but without PSH A:

In short, the "naked ACK" without a "PSH" flag is not a network failure; it is a signal that the Mysql application layer is stalled. The Linux TCP stack is confirming that it successfully received your query (ACK), but the MySQL engine hasn't yet produced a response to "push" back (PSH) because it is busy processing or waiting on a system resource. This 20-second hang during your 2,000-insert burst is likely caused by InnoDB CheckPointing or Redo log flushing. When MySQL's log files or buffer pools fill up with new data, the engine occasionally freezes all incoming writes to flush dirty pages to the disk. To fix this, you should increase your innodb_log_file_size and ensure your binary uses the TCP_NODELAY socket option to prevent the Linux kernel from buffering small packets

Q: Why is there an infinite chain of `.prototype.constructor` properties? A:

This is a desired behavior. The constructor property of a prototype refers to the object that owns the prototype (so it refers back to itself).

Q: Javascript object members that are prototyped as arrays become shared by all class instances A:

When you do var exp1 = new C(), JavaScript sets exp1.[[Prototype]] = C.prototype. When you then access properties of the instance, JavaScript first checks whether they exist on that object directly, and if not, it looks in [[Prototype]]. This means that all the stuff you define in prototype is effectively shared by all instances, and you can even later change parts of prototype and have the changes appear in all existing instances.

Q: How do I fix the jupyter notebook search box error "TypeError: can't access property "length", child is undefined"? A:

Fix: cut and paste the bad markup cell

There is such an easy fix to this that I had to share this. I came to think of fixing this only after many of these error messages since the notebook is huge, and I could not spend the time on it. But when I found a white space in a cell, it was too likely linked to this bug.

In short: this happens if you deal with special signs in markup cells. It happened a dozen times and always just in the markdown cells, for example:

  • after pasting from the chatbot,
  • and shortly after search-replacing a word with a new word over the whole notebook, and that new word had an umlaut "ä" in it,
  • after replacing an umlaut word with a non-umlaut word.

Clip the whole cell that has white space in it and paste and run it again:

  1. Escx to cut the bad cell,
  2. arrow-up one time, and
  3. Escv to paste it after the cell again.

These three shortcuts work so well that I do no longer check whether the cell end position is right. While pasting the cell, the markdown is compiled. Then, the error is gone at once, without leaving and opening the session.

Finding the "bad markup cell"

If you do not check it at once, it may take a long time to find the bad cell, or you need to reopen the notebook. That is why you should check the cells of the neighbourhood right away when the error pops up at first. Strangely, the cell with the error is often not the one that you see, but the one right below it. Thus, as soon as you see the error in the search box, check the next cell on screen as well by scrolling down a bit.

You may also open the notebook a second time, search for the same search word again, and then find that cell without the help of the the search box in your "broken search box"-notebook.

Quick fix: open the notebook again

In a huge notebook, you do not know where that white space cell is. You need to find it by scrolling or by chance, but you will not have the time for that. That is why it is enough to save, close and open the notebook again, so that you get back the search box. Yet, the search box error will always pop up again during searching, since search will find something in these white boxes or pass them. At best, you just keep your eyes open while working and searching. As soon as you see by chance such a white box again, like the following, you should fix it right away, else you will run into the search box error again.

Workaround: go on without the search box

I often do not want to close my work and lose the variables in memory. I went over to search with my own eyes, without the search box, when this happened in a running project state. This is worth a hint since I was not aware how quickly you can adapt to this. After a while, I knew my code much better. For a short time, this can be done.

================================

Finding out

I found this strange white space by chance:

While the search bar shows this error everywhere, not just when you see this cell, I was still aware that I did not have such two bugs in one go before. They had to be linked. This white space was always at the same point and was likely the reason for the error: roughly since pasting that text, I remember having had this search error once in a while.

Yet, if I run the markdown cell with the white space again, the writing in the white space can be seen again, and there is no special character that can tell why the search error happens:

--clip-grad NORM <----- FROM HERE, THE WHITE SPACE STARTED
Clip gradient norm (default: None, no clipping)

--sched SCHEDULER
LR scheduler (default: "step")

--lr LR
Learning rate, overrides lr-base if set (default: None)

--warmup-lr LR
Warmup learning rate (default: 1e-5)

If I double click to edit the markdown cell, the white space is back, I cannot see or edit the writing after --clip-grad NORM. I cannot even mark any text in the edit mode and therefore cannot clip the text.

My guess: a space sign that is forbidden in markdown. Or something else that makes the text more than a text or a broken text. That would also go along with the Error "TypeError: can't access property "length", child is undefined".

Q: How to read python bytecode? A: 
When you disassemble a Python function using the `dis` module, you see a list of low‑level instructions that the CPython interpreter executes. Each line in the disassembly has three important parts:

1. The bytecode offset  
2. The opcode (e.g., LOAD_CONST, STORE_FAST)  
3. The argument to the opcode, if any

Example:

    0 LOAD_CONST        1 (1)
    3 STORE_FAST        0 (x)
    6 LOAD_CONST        0 (None)
    9 RETURN_VALUE

────────────────────────────────────────
1) Bytecode offsets (0, 3, 6, 9)
These numbers are positions inside the raw bytecode stream.  
Each instruction takes up a certain number of bytes, so the next instruction begins at a new offset.

You can see the raw bytecode with:

```python
func.__code__.co_code
────────────────────────────────────────

LOAD_CONST
This instruction pushes a constant onto the Python VM stack.

LOAD_CONST 1 (1) means:

Look up index 1 in co_consts

Push that value onto the stack

Check the constants:

python
func.__code__.co_consts
# (None, 1)
So index 1 is the integer 1.

────────────────────────────────────────

STORE_FAST
This stores the top‑of‑stack value into a local variable.

STORE_FAST 0 (x) means:

Take the value on top of the stack (1)

Store it in local variable index 0

Local variable names come from:

python
func.__code__.co_varnames
# ('x',)
────────────────────────────────────────

LOAD_CONST 0 (None)
Python automatically loads None because functions without an explicit return statement return None.

────────────────────────────────────────

RETURN_VALUE
This pops the top value from the stack and returns it as the function’s result.

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

Offsets = positions in the bytecode stream

LOAD_CONST = push a constant from co_consts

STORE_FAST = store a value into a local variable

RETURN_VALUE = return the top‑of‑stack value

For a full list of opcodes, see the official Python docs for dis and opcode.

Q: VS2026 legacy solution error - "This version of Visual Studio .NET does not support source controlled projects" A:

Before opening a project/solution with a new version of VS you must check in or reverse all pending changes in the older version. TFS otherwise will prevent saving the project with the new version.
